WHO LBM4 uses an evidence- and risk-based approach in which safety measures are balanced against the actual risk of the activity on a case-by-case basis. core risk approach risk_assessment

Risk assessment requires information on biological hazards, procedures, equipment, facility and human competency; knowledge gaps negatively affect evaluation and control selection. information gathering uncertainty
Risk evaluation considers how exposure/release could occur, likelihood, consequences and whether risks can be controlled to an acceptable level. risk evaluation risk_assessment

WHO's 2024 laboratory biosecurity guidance applies a risk- and evidence-based approach to biosecurity, including governance, secure handling, transport/storage and high-consequence research risk management. 2024 guidance biosecurity

WHO describes biological risk assessment as a systematic process of gathering information and evaluating risks to support risk management. The results of the assessment inform selection of risk control measures, including training and appropriate PPE. Section 1 – Introduction risk_assessment_purpose

In laboratory biosafety, WHO describes a biological hazard as a biological agent whose pathogenic characteristics give it the potential to cause harm to people, animals and/or the environment. Section 1 – Introduction hazard_definition

WHO defines biological risk in context as the combination of the likelihood that an exposure to or release of a biological hazard occurs during laboratory work and the severity of the consequences if that incident occurs. Section 1 – Introduction risk_definition

WHO notes that laboratory biological risk depends on dynamic factors including the procedures performed, equipment available, pathogenic properties of the biological agent, host range, population susceptibility and the competency of laboratory personnel. Section 1 – Introduction risk_factors

WHO risk assessment requires risk control measures to be selected for the specific activity and then considers residual risk and whether the selected measures are available, effective and sustainable. Step 4 – Select and implement risk control measures risk_control_selection

WHO LBM4 uses an evidence- and risk-based approach so that safety measures are balanced against the actual risk of work with biological agents on a case-by-case basis; a proper risk assessment should be performed before activities and should inform risk control measures. Core evidence- and risk-based approach activity_specific_controls

WHO places PPE within broader laboratory biosafety core requirements rather than treating PPE as a complete safety determination. Core requirements include good microbiological practice and procedure, with PPE such as laboratory coats, footwear, gloves and eye protection used as applicable. Section 3 – PPE for core requirements ppe_role

WHO indicates that some PPE needs are determined by risk assessment; for example, respiratory protection for biological agents is not a general core requirement and becomes a heightened control measure when the risk assessment indicates it is needed. Section 3 – PPE for core requirements ppe_risk_based_selection

WHO's risk-based framework does not use PPE alone to establish that an activity is safe: risk assessment determines the control measures needed for the activity, and control selection can include training, PPE, equipment and other containment measures appropriate to the identified risk. Section 1 / risk assessment framework layered_controls

A comprehensive biological risk assessment considers the biological hazard together with how work is performed and the context in which it is performed; relevant information includes procedures, equipment, facility and personnel competency, and the assessment evaluates exposure or release, likelihood and consequences. Risk assessment framework risk_assessment_scope
